sentences.text: Fully grown individuals of Sarcosuchus imperator are estimated to have reached lengths of 9 to 9.5 meters and weights of 3.45 to 4.3 metric tons.
This predator possessed a very long skull with a snout that accounted for 75% of the skull's total length.
Its vertebrae were amphicoelus, a structural feature not found in modern crocodilians or the related group Atoposauridae.
Osteoderms on the neck and back featured low keels and hook-shaped extensions, while those on the tail lacked these specific features.
Unlike other crocodiles, the skull of Sarcosuchus widens distinctly toward the front.
Scale studies suggest that Sarcosuchus reached its adult size at the remarkably old age of 50 to 60 years.
It is considered a generalist predator, a trait that sets it apart from most other pholidosaurids which were specialized fish eaters.
The genus Sarcosuchus was first formally described in 1966 by Frances de Broin and Philippe Taquet based on an incomplete skull found in Gadoufaoua, northern Niger.
Fossils of this creature were initially discovered in the 1850s in Salvador, Bahia, Brazil, by the collector Samuel Allport.
Sarcosuchus was first discovered in 1947 by French paleontologist Félix de Lapparent, who found conical teeth, vertebrae, and foot scales.
In 1977, the species formerly known as Crocodylus hartti was reassigned to the genus Sarcosuchus.
That same year, Philippe Taquet and Eric Buffetaut reassigned Goniopholis hartti to Sarcosuchus based on similarities in teeth, jaws, and osteoderms.
Isotopic analyses suggest that S. imperator had a diet consisting of both fish and large dinosaurs.
Researchers hypothesized that Sarcosuchus imperator had a generalized diet including large terrestrial prey like dinosaurs.
Sarcosuchus fed on fish and small to medium-sized dinosaurs caught in waterways.
The morphology of Sarcosuchus was similar to that of modern gharials.
Biomechanical analyses indicate that Sarcosuchus was not capable of performing a crocodile-like 'death roll'.
O'Brien et al. (2019) estimated the largest S. imperator specimen was nearly 9 meters long and weighed 3.45 metric tons.
The genus Sarcosuchus includes the type species Sarcosuchus imperator.
Sarcosuchus is classified within the clade Pholidosauridae, which is related to but distinct from the group containing modern crocodiles and alligators.
Sarcosuchus is most closely related to the North American genus Terminonaris.
A 2019 study placed Sarcosuchus phylogenetically closer to Dyrosauridae within the group Tethysuchia.
Sarcosuchus is classified in the family Pholidosauridae.
Sarcosuchus lived during the Early Cretaceous, specifically the Hauterivian to Albian ages, in North Africa and Brazil.
The Gadoufaoua locality, where Sarcosuchus fossils were found, dates to between 125 and 112 million years ago.
During the Early Cretaceous, North Africa and Brazil were covered in mangrove forests and wetlands, creating a biodiversity hotspot.
Sarcosuchus coexisted with theropod dinosaurs and other crocodiles, living near river banks.
Sarcosuchus coexisted with large sauropods such as Paralititan.
The time range for the genus Sarcosuchus is from the Valanginian to the Cenomanian (137.05 to 93.9 million years ago).
It is debated whether Sarcosuchus had a lifestyle similar to the Nile crocodile, hunting large terrestrial prey.
Some researchers argue that estimates of S. imperator size based on modern crocodilian correlations are significantly larger than reality.
